entities.name: International Energy Agency
entities.definition: Organization created in 1974 specifically because the 1973 OPEC embargo nearly toppled Western economies — activated the system it was built for during the 2026 Hormuz crisis by coordinating the largest strategic petroleum reserve release in its 52-year history (400 million barrels across 31 nations).

projectRoles.project: The Strait of Hormuz: Military Chokepoint That Broke Global Energy
projectRoles.role: The institutional response mechanism born from the same 1973 crisis that created the petrodollar system. The IEA's stance is coordinated energy security. The mechanics: (1) created in direct response to the 1973 OPEC embargo, (2) coordinates strategic reserve releases among 31 member nations, (3) activated the largest release in its history during the 2026 Hormuz crisis, (4) but the IEA system was designed for supply disruptions, not for insurance-driven closures — no reserve release can address the actuarial mechanism that actually closed the strait. The IEA represents the pattern: each crisis produces institutions designed to prevent the next one, but each institution proves insufficient when the next crisis arrives.

entities.name: Offshore Banking Network
entities.definition: Global network of jurisdictions following the Hong Kong blueprint: favorable regulation, foreign or alternative legal systems, geographic or jurisdictional distance from the authorities whose rules the money is avoiding. Nodes include Hong Kong (the original), Singapore, Cayman Islands ($1.5 trillion in deposits, 100,000 registered companies), Jersey ($300 billion in banking assets), British Virgin Islands (400,000 registered companies for 30,000 people), Luxembourg ($5 trillion in fund assets), and Delaware (anonymous company registration).

projectRoles.role: The scaled output of the opium equation's permanent infrastructure variable, replicated across the globe. The network's role is to provide jurisdictional arbitrage at industrial scale: each node offers the same value proposition Hong Kong pioneered -- a space where capital can move with minimal regulatory friction, where ownership can be obscured, and where the laws of the jurisdiction generating the money do not apply. The mechanics are identical at every node: favorable tax treatment attracts capital, foreign legal systems provide certainty for international actors, geographic or legal distance from regulatory authorities prevents scrutiny, and the network effect of multiple connected nodes makes the system self-reinforcing and impossible to dismantle without dismantling global commerce itself.

entities.name: Veolia
entities.definition: French multinational water corporation reporting water division revenue of eleven point four billion euros with a seven percent growth target — one of the two dominant global water companies whose annual report uses the word 'opportunity' to describe the same water that UNICEF's report describes as 'crisis' — responsible for eight hundred twenty-nine thousand deaths annually from waterborne disease.

projectRoles.role: The other French corporate pillar of global water privatization, alongside Suez. Veolia's stance is shareholder-return-driven water management. The mechanics: (1) water division generates 11.4 billion euros annually, (2) growth targets of 7% require expanding into new markets — meaning more cities privatizing water, (3) the same resource appears in two documents with opposite framing: Veolia's annual report calls it opportunity, UNICEF calls it crisis, (4) like Suez, headquartered in France — whose capital Paris re-municipalized water. The companies that sold privatization to the developing world couldn't sell it to their own citizens.

entities.name: David Sassoon & Sons
entities.definition: Opium trading dynasty founded by David Sassoon (Baghdadi Jewish merchant, arrived Bombay 1832) that built the largest opium trading operation in Asia by the 1870s, extending networks across Shanghai, Hong Kong, Canton, and Calcutta. Was a founding shareholder of HSBC. Within two generations, the family acquired London townhouses, country estates, baronetcies, and parliamentary seats -- Siegfried Sassoon wrote defining WWI poetry, Philip Sassoon served in the British Cabinet.

projectRoles.role: The most complete case study of the legitimacy machine at work. The Sassoons demonstrate the mechanics of how drug wealth converts to aristocratic status: (1) accumulate through narcotics trading at industrial scale, (2) diversify into legitimate holdings, (3) acquire social markers (property, titles, political office), (4) wait one to two generations until the origin becomes 'history' rather than 'crime.' The money did not become clean -- it became old. And old money is clean money by definition. This pattern is structural, not unique to the Sassoons: it is the universal mechanism by which illicit wealth achieves legitimacy.

entities.name: Monoculture
entities.definition: Agricultural practice of growing a single crop in dense plantings — required by Green Revolution varieties and opposite of traditional polyculture — creating 'buffets for pests' that require chemical pesticide intervention, while eliminating the natural pest suppression of diverse interplanting.

projectRoles.role: The agricultural method that creates pesticide dependency. Monoculture's mechanics: (1) Green Revolution wheat grows in dense single-crop plantings, (2) monocultures concentrate pest populations — 'buffets for pests,' (3) traditional polyculture (dozens of crops interplanted) naturally suppresses pests, (4) monoculture requires chemical intervention — 'this farmer is spraying organophosphates without protective equipment. He does this every season. The chemicals enter the soil, the water, his lungs. This is not an accident. It is a feature of the system.'

entities.name: Aquifer Depletion
entities.definition: The progressive exhaustion of Punjab's ancient aquifer by tube wells drilled to irrigate Green Revolution crops — wells going from fifty feet to four hundred feet deep over decades as the water table drops, with NASA satellite data confirming northwestern India's groundwater is depleting at one of the fastest rates on Earth.

projectRoles.role: The ecological time bomb beneath the Green Revolution's success. The aquifer depletion's mechanics: (1) semi-dwarf wheat needs precise water — not too much, not too little, (2) tube wells drilled into millennia-old aquifer, (3) extraction exceeds recharge — wells go deeper each year (50 → 100 → 200 → 400 feet), (4) 'the aquifer doesn't know about crop schedules — it just knows extraction,' (5) 'when it's gone, it's gone. And it is going.' We are farming on ecological credit — the land that saved India from famine is being hollowed out from beneath.

entities.name: Victor Hugo Daza
entities.definition: Seventeen-year-old Bolivian boy shot through the face by a military sniper on April 8, 2000 during the Cochabamba Water War — not a protester but a bystander walking past, killed on a street named after Simon Bolivar the liberator — whose death became the turning point that ended Bechtel's water concession and symbolized the human cost of water privatization.

projectRoles.role: The human cost made visible. Victor Hugo Daza's death is the investigation's moral anchor — one boy, one bullet, fired on behalf of a water company headquartered four thousand miles away. His significance is that he was NOT a protester — he was walking past. The mechanics of his death trace directly to institutional decisions: World Bank required privatization, Bolivia accepted the condition, Bechtel raised prices, people protested, the government deployed snipers, a boy died. The causal chain from loan condition to bullet is unbroken.

entities.name: Lin Zexu
entities.definition: Imperial Chinese commissioner appointed to enforce China's opium prohibition (law since 1729), who destroyed 20,000 chests of British-owned opium worth $350 million (modern value) at Humen Beach in June 1839, wrote a devastating moral appeal to Queen Victoria exposing British hypocrisy on drug policy, and whose enforcement action directly triggered the First Opium War and China's subsequent military defeat.

projectRoles.role: The moral antagonist to the opium system who exposed its fundamental nature through failure. Lin Zexu's stance was that drug law enforcement was a sovereign right and that moral reasoning could persuade the British Crown to cease the trade. His mechanics were legally sound -- destroying contraband, writing reasoned diplomatic appeals -- but his fundamental error was addressing the British system as a moral actor rather than a revenue-extraction machine. His defeat demonstrated that moral appeals to revenue systems produce, at best, public relations responses, and that enforcing drug laws against militarily superior narco-states results in punishment of the enforcing nation.

entities.name: Fertilizer Cascade
entities.definition: The hidden branch of the Hormuz crisis most analysts miss — one-third of global fertilizer trade transits the strait (Qatar nitrogen/urea, Saudi/UAE/Oman phosphates/potash), with New Orleans benchmark prices spiking 43% ($475 to $680/metric ton), propagating to food prices with a 3-6 month lag that transforms an energy crisis into a food crisis hitting the same vulnerable populations.

projectRoles.project: The Strait of Hormuz: Military Chokepoint That Broke Global Energy
projectRoles.role: The demonstration that Hormuz is simultaneously an energy crisis and a food crisis on a delayed timeline. The fertilizer cascade's stance is hidden interconnection. The mechanics: (1) one-third of global fertilizer trade transits Hormuz — a fact most analysts miss, (2) Qatar is a top global nitrogen fertilizer producer, (3) nitrogen prices spiked 43% at the New Orleans benchmark, (4) fertilizer price → food price with 3-6 month lag (planting to harvest), (5) countries importing the most fertilizer and least able to afford shocks — Egypt (60% wheat imports), Bangladesh, Sub-Saharan Africa, Philippines — face food insecurity. The energy cascade and food cascade are the same cascade, running through the same chokepoint, hitting the same populations without strategic reserves.

entities.name: Re-municipalization Movement
entities.definition: Global counter-movement in which at least 235 cities in 37 countries have taken their water systems back from private operators since 2000 — including Paris, home city of Suez and Veolia — representing the largest reversal of water privatization and proving that the French companies selling privatization to the developing world couldn't sell it to their own capital.

projectRoles.role: The evidence that privatization is reversible and that communities can take water back. The movement's mechanics: (1) 235 cities in 37 countries since 2000, (2) Paris re-municipalized — the home city of the two largest water corporations, (3) the French companies that sold privatization to the developing world couldn't sell it to their own capital, (4) the movement is part of the 'light side' of the investigation's final image — alongside Cochabamba's La Coordinadora, UN Resolution 64/292, community water cooperatives, and indigenous water protectors.

entities.name: Digital Yuan
entities.definition: China's central bank digital currency that has processed $2.38 trillion in cumulative transactions through 2.25 billion wallets — as of 2026 paying interest — giving China's central bank the ability to see every transaction, adjust money supply in real time, and potentially program how money is spent.

projectRoles.role: The most advanced CBDC in the world and the technology embodying state-maximalist digital money. The digital yuan gives the PBOC capabilities no previous central bank possessed: real-time transaction visibility, programmable spending restrictions, and instant money supply adjustment. It represents one model for the future of money — government-issued, fully surveilled, centrally controllable.

entities.name: Strategic Petroleum Reserves
entities.definition: Emergency oil stockpiles held by 31 IEA member nations — 400 million barrels released in the largest coordinated drawdown in the IEA's 52-year history — that represent 20 days of Hormuz traffic and require 13 days from presidential order to market delivery, making them a slow weapon against a fast crisis that buys time but cannot substitute for the strait.

projectRoles.project: The Strait of Hormuz: Military Chokepoint That Broke Global Energy
projectRoles.role: The emergency buffer that proves the system's fragility rather than its resilience. SPR's stance is temporary relief. The mechanics: (1) 400M barrels released — largest in IEA history, larger than Libya 2011 or Russia-Ukraine 2022, (2) equals only 20 days of Hormuz flows — weeks of buffer, not months, (3) US SPR requires ~13 days from presidential order to market delivery through pipelines and refining, (4) Japan holds 140 days (adequate for weeks), South Korea 90 days (3 months), India and developing nations have minimal reserves. The reserves reveal the timeline: if the strait stays closed for a month they buy time; three months, a slower crisis; six months, they run out and the world enters territory no economic model has ever been tested against.

entities.name: Oil Embargo of 1973
entities.definition: OPEC retaliation against US support for Israel during the Yom Kippur War, quadrupling crude prices from $3 to $12/barrel and bringing the American economy to its knees — the crisis that revealed oil's true power as the 'blood supply of industrial civilization' and created the conditions Kissinger exploited to forge the petrodollar pact.

projectRoles.role: The catalytic crisis that made the petrodollar possible. The embargo's stance was geopolitical retaliation, but its systemic effect was revealing oil's leverage over industrial civilization. The mechanics: (1) Arab nations attacked Israel in the Yom Kippur War, (2) the US resupplied Israel with weapons, (3) OPEC retaliated with an embargo that quadrupled oil prices, (4) gas stations ran dry, lines stretched around blocks, speed limits dropped to 55, the US economy buckled. Kissinger's genius was seeing this not as a problem but as an 'anchor' — proof that whoever controlled oil pricing controlled the global financial architecture. The crisis created both the leverage (oil is power) and the urgency (the dollar needs a new anchor) for the 1974 pact.

entities.name: Bank of England
entities.definition: The world's first central bank, created in 1694 when a group of London merchants lent King William III £1.2 million at 8% interest to fight France, receiving in exchange the right to issue banknotes backed by government debt — establishing the template that central banks are born not to stabilize economies but to fund wars.
aliases: The Old Lady of Threadneedle Street

projectRoles.role: The origin template for all central banking. The Bank of England established the foundational pattern: (1) created to fund a war, not stabilize an economy, (2) merchants lend to the state in exchange for money-creation privileges, (3) the money is raised in eleven days — demonstrating that private capital and state power combine when mutual interest aligns. This pattern repeats for three centuries across every major central bank.

entities.name: Cold War
entities.definition: Global geopolitical conflict between the US and Soviet Union that provided the strategic motivation for the Green Revolution — making agricultural development a tool of political alignment where 'we feed you, you align with us' was the operating logic behind food aid and agricultural modernization programs.

projectRoles.role: The geopolitical context that transformed agricultural science into foreign policy. The Cold War's role in the investigation: (1) Food for Peace program tied wheat exports to political alignment, (2) Johnson's 'short-tether diplomacy' used famine as geopolitical leverage, (3) preventing communist revolution in hungry nations was an explicit motivation, (4) the Cold War appears on the convergence map as the strategic motivation layer beneath the humanitarian narrative.

entities.name: Food for Peace
entities.definition: American food aid program under which India imported wheat in the 1960s — where 'peace' meant geopolitical alignment: 'we feed you, you align with us' — the legislative mechanism through which famine was leveraged for Cold War foreign policy objectives.

projectRoles.role: The legal instrument that weaponized food aid. Food for Peace's mechanics: the name says peace but the function is alignment — American wheat exports to India were conditioned on political cooperation, making famine a lever for geopolitical influence during the Cold War.

entities.name: European Central Bank
entities.definition: Institution managing monetary policy for the nineteen countries sharing the euro, whose president Mario Draghi demonstrated the power of central bank communication when six words — 'whatever it takes to preserve the euro' — ended the 2012 eurozone crisis without spending a single euro. Holds rates at 2.0% in March 2026 with eurozone inflation at 1.7%.

projectRoles.role: Demonstrates the purest form of central bank power: the ability to move markets with words alone. The ECB under Draghi proved that credibility IS the tool — three words did the work that trillions in bond purchases might not have. In 2026, under Lagarde, the ECB faces stagnation rather than inflation, illustrating that different central banks face completely different problems within one interconnected system.

entities.name: Paul Warburg
entities.definition: German-born banker at Kuhn, Loeb & Co. who had studied the Reichsbank and the Bank of England — the international banking expert among the Jekyll Island six who brought European central banking models to the American design.

projectRoles.role: The intellectual architect who imported European central banking expertise to America. Warburg's knowledge of the Reichsbank and Bank of England provided the structural template — the Federal Reserve was not designed from American principles but adapted from European models by a banker who understood both systems.

entities.name: Alexander Hamilton
entities.definition: First Secretary of the Treasury who created the First Bank of the United States in 1791, establishing America's first experiment with central banking against fierce opposition from Thomas Jefferson who saw it as an unconstitutional concentration of financial power.

projectRoles.role: The first American advocate for central banking. Hamilton's creation of the First Bank established the pro-centralization position in a debate that would continue for 120 years: centralized financial power enables economic coordination but concentrates control. Jefferson's opposition defined the counter-argument that runs through the investigation.

entities.name: Thomas Jefferson
entities.definition: Third President of the United States who opposed Hamilton's First Bank as an unconstitutional concentration of financial power — establishing the anti-central-bank position that Andrew Jackson would weaponize and that echoes in 2026 debates over Federal Reserve independence.

projectRoles.role: The voice of opposition to centralized financial power. Jefferson's constitutional argument against the First Bank is the investigation's recurring tension: the democratic objection that unelected institutions should not control the money supply. This argument reappears with Jackson, is dormant during the Federal Reserve era, and resurfaces in 2026.

entities.name: Andrew Jackson
entities.definition: Seventh President of the United States who killed the Second Bank of the United States in 1836 — withdrawing all federal deposits with the declaration 'The Bank is trying to kill me, but I will kill it' — leaving America without a central bank for seventy-seven years.

projectRoles.role: The most aggressive opponent of central banking in American history. Jackson's destruction of the Second Bank created the seventy-seven-year gap (1836-1913) during which America was the only major industrial economy without a central bank — proving that the country could function without one, but at the cost of every financial panic requiring private resolution.

entities.name: Mario Draghi
entities.definition: President of the European Central Bank who in July 2012, with the eurozone fracturing and Greek, Italian, and Spanish bond yields spiking, spoke six words — 'Whatever it takes to preserve the euro' — that collapsed bond yields and ended the crisis without the ECB spending a single euro, demonstrating that central bank credibility is itself a tool.

projectRoles.role: The most dramatic demonstration of forward guidance power. Draghi proved that a central banker's words can substitute for trillions in actual spending: (1) markets were pricing in the euro's collapse, (2) six words reversed that pricing, (3) the ECB spent nothing. Three words did the work. This moment demonstrates that central bank power is ultimately about credibility — and that credibility, once established, is the most efficient monetary tool.

entities.name: Jerome Powell
entities.definition: Federal Reserve Chair whose term expires May 15, 2026, holding rates at 3.50-3.75% with US inflation stubbornly at 2.4% above the 2% target — the person at the center of the 2026 independence crisis as President Trump nominates Kevin Warsh to replace him.

projectRoles.role: The focal point of the 2026 independence test. Powell's situation crystallizes the investigation's central tension: (1) he holds rates based on technocratic judgment, (2) the president wants to replace him with his own nominee, (3) the independence of the Federal Reserve is being tested more directly than at any point since Nixon. Whether Powell's successor serves the economy or the incumbent is the open question.

entities.name: Recep Tayyip Erdogan
entities.definition: President of Turkey who fired multiple central bank governors who tried to raise rates, believing high interest rates cause inflation — the opposite of mainstream economics — producing Turkish inflation of 34.9% and serving as the cautionary tale for what happens when political leaders capture central bank policy.

projectRoles.role: The cautionary tale of political capture. Erdogan demonstrates Path B of the investigation's futures: (1) president overrides central bank, (2) fires governors who disagree, (3) implements heterodox policy (low rates to fight inflation), (4) inflation hits 34.9%. Turkey is the real-world evidence for why central bank independence exists — and what happens when it doesn't.

entities.name: Donald Trump
entities.definition: President of the United States who in January 2026 nominated Kevin Warsh to replace Jerome Powell as Fed Chair and placed Stephen Miran on the Fed Board — testing the independence of the Federal Reserve more directly than at any point since Nixon's era.

projectRoles.role: The American vector of the global independence challenge. Trump's actions — replacing the Fed Chair with his own nominee, placing allies on the Fed Board — represent the most direct presidential attempt to influence Federal Reserve policy in decades. Whether this constitutes legitimate appointment power or political capture of monetary policy is the investigation's 2026 question.

entities.name: Kevin Warsh
entities.definition: President Trump's nominee to replace Jerome Powell as Federal Reserve Chair, whose confirmation has been blocked by Senator Thom Tillis over a Department of Justice investigation of Powell — placing the Fed's leadership transition at the intersection of presidential politics and congressional procedure.

projectRoles.role: The person at the center of the 2026 Fed succession crisis. Warsh's blocked nomination demonstrates that the independence question is not just executive versus central bank — Congress has its own leverage through confirmation power, creating a three-way power struggle over who controls monetary policy.

entities.name: Thom Tillis
entities.definition: US Senator who blocked Kevin Warsh's confirmation as Federal Reserve Chair over a Department of Justice investigation of Jerome Powell — inserting congressional power into the Fed succession process and complicating the president's attempt to install his preferred central banker.

projectRoles.role: The congressional check on presidential Fed appointments. Tillis's blocking action demonstrates that the Fed independence system has multiple institutional safeguards — even when a president wants to replace the Fed Chair, Senate confirmation creates a veto point that can be exercised for institutional or political reasons.

entities.name: Reichsbank
entities.definition: Germany's central bank studied by Paul Warburg before the Jekyll Island meeting — one of the European models that informed the Federal Reserve's design, demonstrating that America's central bank was adapted from European templates rather than designed from scratch.

projectRoles.role: One of the European models imported to America through Warburg. The Reichsbank's structure — along with the Bank of England's — provided the institutional template that the Jekyll Island six adapted for the American context.

entities.name: Department of Justice
entities.definition: Federal law enforcement agency whose investigation of Jerome Powell became the basis for Senator Thom Tillis blocking Kevin Warsh's confirmation as Fed Chair — introducing criminal investigation dynamics into the central bank succession process.

projectRoles.role: The legal institution whose investigation intersects with Fed appointments. The DOJ's role in the Warsh blockade demonstrates that the central bank independence system involves multiple institutional actors — not just the president and the central bank, but Congress and law enforcement as well.

The enforcement authority that articulated and operationalized the 'too big to jail' doctrine, demonstrating the limits of legal accountability when confronting permanently embedded financial infrastructure. The DOJ's stance was that systemic stability outweighed criminal accountability: the bank's $1.9 billion fine (less than nine days of $80 billion annual revenue) represented a cost-of-business model rather than deterrence. The mechanics reveal that the opium equation's endgame is structural impunity: once the infrastructure built for drug money becomes the infrastructure everyone depends on, the builder cannot be prosecuted without damaging the system itself.

entities.name: Second Bank of the United States
entities.definition: America's second central bank, chartered in 1816 and killed by Andrew Jackson in 1836 when he withdrew all federal deposits — leaving the United States without a central bank for seventy-seven years, the only major industrial economy without one.

projectRoles.role: The institution whose death created the gap that led to the Federal Reserve. Jackson's destruction of the Second Bank proved America could function without a central bank — but at the cost of requiring private actors (ultimately J.P. Morgan) to resolve every financial crisis. The seventy-seven-year gap is what made Jekyll Island politically necessary.

entities.name: Central Bank Independence
entities.definition: The doctrine that politicians cannot be trusted with the money supply — that independent central bankers appointed for long terms and insulated from electoral pressure can make unpopular decisions like raising rates when politicians want them low — governing central banking for four decades but containing a democratic tension that has never been fully resolved.

projectRoles.role: The investigation's central doctrine under attack. Independence rests on the logic: (1) presidents want cheap money before elections, (2) inflationary consequences arrive after, (3) independent central bankers can make unpopular decisions. But the counter-argument is equally powerful: the most consequential economic decisions affecting hundreds of millions are made by officials nobody elected, using tools nobody voted on, with mandates nobody can recall. Turkey shows what happens without independence. The democratic deficit shows what happens with it.

entities.name: SWIFT
entities.definition: Dollar-based international banking messaging system that underpins global financial transactions, whose importance as a sanctions weapon was demonstrated when Russia was disconnected in 2022 — freezing $300 billion in central bank reserves and proving that dollar infrastructure doubles as a geopolitical enforcement tool.
aliases: Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication

projectRoles.role: The financial plumbing that enables dollar-based sanctions. SWIFT's stance is as neutral infrastructure, but its function is inseparable from dollar dominance. The mechanics: (1) virtually all international banking transactions route through SWIFT, (2) because the system runs on dollars, disconnection from SWIFT means disconnection from the global economy, (3) when Russia was cut off in 2022, $300 billion in reserves were frozen and its economy was severely constrained, (4) this same weapon was used against Iran (2012), Venezuela, North Korea, Syria, and Cuba. The unintended consequence: SWIFT weaponization now incentivizes alternatives like China's CIPS (1,400+ member institutions by 2024).

entities.name: CIPS
entities.definition: China's alternative to the US-dominated SWIFT international payment system, with over 1,400 member institutions by 2024 — operational infrastructure for cross-border settlements that bypass dollar intermediation entirely, representing tangible progress toward a post-petrodollar financial architecture.

projectRoles.role: The alternative plumbing being built to enable de-dollarization. CIPS's stance is as neutral infrastructure, but its function is to make dollar-free international transactions possible. The mechanics: (1) over 1,400 member institutions by 2024, (2) enables direct yuan-denominated cross-border payments without routing through dollar-based SWIFT, (3) works alongside bilateral currency swap lines (China has 40+ countries), mBridge CBDC connections, and local currency settlement agreements. The key insight: systems don't change when people want them to — they change when the plumbing exists for the alternative. CIPS is that plumbing, being built quietly and functionally while the old system still runs.

entities.name: Surcharge System
entities.definition: Additional interest charged on IMF loans exceeding size (>187.5% of quota) or duration (>36 months) thresholds — currently paid by 22 countries (3x pre-COVID), of which 11 are climate-vulnerable and 12 in debt distress — including Ukraine, projected to pay $2.9 billion in surcharges between 2024-2033 while fighting a full-scale war.

projectRoles.project: The IMF: Lender of Last Resort
projectRoles.role: The extraction mechanism that punishes the most vulnerable borrowers for needing the most help. The surcharge system's stance is repayment incentive through premium pricing. The mechanics: (1) stated purpose is to incentivize quick repayment and discourage excessive borrowing, (2) reality: the countries paying surcharges are precisely those in deepest crisis — the overlap between surcharge-paying, climate-vulnerable, and debt-distressed countries is nearly total, (3) November 2024 reform lowered margin from 100bp to 60bp and raised threshold — estimated savings $1.2B/year, but $9.8B in surcharges still projected over 5 years, (4) Ukraine paying premium charges while its cities are under bombardment is the reductio ad absurdum. The reform reduced the extraction. It did not end it.

entities.name: Ukraine
entities.definition: Nation fighting a full-scale war since February 2022 while simultaneously borrowing from the IMF and projected to pay $2.9 billion in surcharges between 2024-2033 — the most extreme illustration of the surcharge system's perversity, where a country defending its existence pays premium charges to the institution created to stabilize the global financial system.

projectRoles.project: The IMF: Lender of Last Resort
projectRoles.role: The reductio ad absurdum of the surcharge system. Ukraine's stance is survival borrowing under impossible conditions. The mechanics: (1) fighting a full-scale war requires massive borrowing, (2) the borrowing exceeds surcharge thresholds, (3) therefore a country under bombardment pays premium interest to the global stabilization institution, (4) the November 2024 reform reduced but did not eliminate surcharges for countries like Ukraine. Ukraine proves that the surcharge system cannot distinguish between reckless borrowing and existential necessity — it charges the same premium regardless.

entities.name: Cape Town
entities.definition: South African city that in 2018 faced 'Day Zero' — the projected date when municipal taps would shut off entirely — revealing how decades of infrastructure underfunding meant the poor, predominantly Black communities of the Cape Flats had been living in water poverty long before the middle class noticed, while wealthy suburbs tapped private boreholes to different aquifers.

projectRoles.role: The case study of water inequality during scarcity. Cape Town demonstrates how crisis exposes pre-existing stratification. The mechanics: (1) countdown clocks on every news channel for Day Zero, (2) residents queue with containers at municipal water points — 25 liters per person, armed guards monitoring, (3) wealthy suburbs drill private boreholes to different aquifers — same drought, different water source, (4) crisis blamed on climate, but infrastructure had been underfunded for decades, (5) poor Black communities of Cape Flats had been in water poverty already. 'Day Zero was new for some. It was Tuesday for others.'

entities.name: South Africa
entities.definition: Country where Cape Town's 2018 Day Zero water crisis revealed decades of infrastructure underfunding and racial stratification in water access — where poor, predominantly Black communities of the Cape Flats had been living in water poverty long before the middle class noticed, while wealthy suburbs drilled private boreholes to different aquifers during the same drought.

projectRoles.role: The case demonstrating how water crises expose pre-existing inequality along racial and economic lines. South Africa's mechanics: (1) decades of infrastructure underfunding, (2) predominantly Black communities already in water poverty, (3) crisis blamed on climate but structural causes predate drought, (4) wealthy suburbs access different aquifers through private boreholes — same drought, different water, (5) Day Zero was new for some, Tuesday for others. The country demonstrates that water inequality is not produced by scarcity — scarcity merely reveals inequality that was always there.

entities.name: Too Big to Jail
entities.definition: Doctrine articulated by the US Department of Justice in the 2012 HSBC case, holding that criminal prosecution of HSBC could destabilize the global financial system and therefore the bank would face a $1.9 billion fine (less than nine days of revenue) rather than criminal charges, license revocation, or executive arrests. The doctrine demonstrates that financial infrastructure becomes unprosecutable once sufficiently embedded in the global economy.

projectRoles.role: The three words that explain the opium equation better than the entire investigation. The doctrine reveals the endgame of permanent infrastructure: when the pipes built for drug money become the pipes everyone else depends on, the builder of those pipes achieves structural impunity. The mechanics are self-reinforcing: the more embedded the infrastructure becomes, the more damage its removal would cause, the less likely prosecution becomes, the more the infrastructure grows. HSBC's $1.9 billion fine on $80 billion annual revenue demonstrates that the cost of compliance failure is a rounding error while the infrastructure remains intact and continues to process whatever flows through it.

entities.name: Ogallala Aquifer
entities.definition: Massive aquifer beneath the American Great Plains spanning eight states and 174,000 square miles — irrigating twenty billion dollars of agriculture annually — that took millions of years to fill but is being emptied in decades with extraction exceeding recharge by 6:1 in some areas, with parts projected to be functionally dry within thirty years.

projectRoles.role: The ticking resource clock that makes water scarcity concrete. The Ogallala's significance is the arithmetic of depletion: (1) millions of years to fill, decades to empty, (2) extraction rate exceeds recharge 6:1, (3) irrigates $20 billion agriculture annually, (4) when the water runs out, farms stop, food chain breaks, everything downstream breaks. The investigation frames this as 'not a future scenario — this is current hydrology.' The Ogallala makes abstract water scarcity into measurable, predictable collapse.

entities.name: Input Stack
entities.definition: The interlocking set of purchased inputs required by Green Revolution crop varieties — synthetic fertilizer (petroleum-derived), chemical pesticides (from former wartime munitions manufacturers), controlled irrigation (from wells drilled with borrowed money), and credit (from banks connected to institutions with their own agendas) — where 'the seed is the app and this is the operating system.'

projectRoles.role: The hidden architecture that transforms a seed breakthrough into an economic trap. The input stack's mechanics: (1) each component is necessary — the seed cannot produce high yields without all four inputs, (2) each component requires cash before planting, transforming farming from a largely self-sufficient activity to a credit-dependent business, (3) each component is supplied by external actors (chemical companies, banks, well drillers), (4) every dependency is a revenue stream for someone who isn't farming. The input stack is what turns the Green Revolution from a technology into an operating system.

entities.name: Sri Lanka
entities.definition: Nation that has entered 17 IMF programs since 1965 — the investigation's primary case study of the revolving door — culminating in its first-ever sovereign default in April 2022 when reserves fell below $50 million, followed by fuel shortages, power cuts, hospital medicine shortages, citizens storming the presidential palace, and the president fleeing by military aircraft, before the IMF arrived again.

projectRoles.project: The IMF: Lender of Last Resort
projectRoles.role: The pattern incarnate — one country, one lender, sixty years, the same cycle. Sri Lanka's stance is structural dependency on an institution that treats symptoms without resolving causes. The mechanics: (1) 17 programs since 1965 — each time the country ran out of money, called the IMF, agreed to conditions, and eventually repeated the cycle, (2) the 2022 default was the bottom: reserves below $50M, 12-hour power cuts, Rajapaksa fleeing by helicopter, (3) then Cyclone Ditwah in November 2025 killed 643 people and displaced 2.2 million while the country was mid-program, (4) a nation contributing <0.1% of global carbon emissions pays premium charges on emergency loans while absorbing the worst climate impacts. Sri Lanka is the proof that conditional lending treating symptoms without curing structural causes guarantees return customers.

entities.name: Bolivia
entities.definition: South American nation that became the epicenter of the global water privatization conflict in 2000 — where the collision between World Bank conditionality, corporate profit extraction, military repression, and popular resistance produced the Cochabamba Water War, the most studied case of water privatization failure and the catalyst for the global water justice movement.

projectRoles.role: The battleground where all the system's contradictions became visible. Bolivia's stance was initially compliant (needed the loan, accepted conditions) then violently repressive (declared state of siege, deployed military snipers) then responsive (cancelled the Bechtel contract after Victor Hugo Daza's death). The mechanics: a country where average income was two dollars a day was forced to privatize water as a loan condition, creating a situation where a family of five earning sixty dollars a month was charged twenty dollars for water alone. The math was never supposed to work for the population — it was designed to work for the creditor and the concessionaire.

entities.name: Jardine Matheson
entities.definition: Private opium trading firm that purchased processed opium at East India Company auctions in Calcutta and smuggled it into China, serving as one of the intermediaries that gave the Company deniability. Was a founding shareholder of HSBC in 1865. Transformed from opium smuggler to Hong Kong blue-chip corporation, demonstrating the legitimacy machine: sufficient wealth applied over sufficient time produces respectability regardless of origin.

projectRoles.role: Key intermediary in the opium distribution chain and founding shareholder of the financial infrastructure that outlived the trade. Jardine Matheson's trajectory from drug smuggler to blue-chip corporation exemplifies the investigation's core thesis: the system does not ask where the money came from, only how much there is and how long it has been compounding. The mechanics of this transformation required no active laundering -- time itself was the laundering mechanism, converting drug profits into diversified investments, real estate, shipping, and corporate respectability.

entities.name: British Empire
entities.definition: Sovereign power that chartered the East India Company, deployed naval force to enforce opium market access in the Opium Wars, imposed the Treaty of Nanking on China, claimed Hong Kong as a colonial jurisdiction, and provided the legal-commercial framework (English commercial law, Lloyd's insurance, the pound sterling) that structured the London-Hong Kong financial corridor. The empire's role was to provide the sovereign authority and military capability that converted commercial drug trafficking into state policy.

projectRoles.role: The sovereign infrastructure behind the opium system, providing the military force, legal framework, and imperial authority that elevated drug trafficking from criminal enterprise to state-sponsored commerce. The British Empire's stance was that free trade -- including narcotics -- was a right enforceable by military means. The mechanics: the Crown chartered the East India Company (granting it quasi-sovereign powers including military force), the Royal Navy supplemented Company forces in the Opium Wars, Parliament debated but ultimately supported the trade, and British commercial law provided the legal certainty that made Hong Kong viable as an offshore financial center. The empire did not merely profit from the opium trade; it was the operating system on which the trade ran.

entities.name: USS Samuel B. Roberts
entities.definition: US guided-missile frigate that struck an Iranian M-08 contact mine on April 14, 1988 while escorting reflagged Kuwaiti tankers during Operation Earnest Will — the mine strike ripped a 15-foot hull hole and broke the ship's keel, directly triggering Operation Praying Mantis and demonstrating that a mine costing thousands of dollars can threaten a vessel worth hundreds of millions.

projectRoles.project: The Strait of Hormuz: Military Chokepoint That Broke Global Energy
projectRoles.role: The physical proof that asymmetric mine warfare works. The Roberts incident demonstrated the core asymmetry: (1) a mine costing a few thousand dollars nearly sank a $200M+ warship, (2) serial numbers matched mines previously seized from an Iranian barge — attribution was clear but prevention was impossible, (3) the same tactic remained viable 38 years later because mines can be laid from indistinguishable fishing boats. The Roberts is the case study that validates Iran's entire asymmetric doctrine: you don't need to match American naval power if a single mine can stop the world's most expensive warships.

entities.name: Sanctions Weapon
entities.definition: The US ability to deny any country access to the global financial system by leveraging dollar dominance — demonstrated against Iran (2012, exports dropped from 2.5M to 500K barrels/day), Russia (2022, $300B frozen), Venezuela, North Korea, Syria, and Cuba — functioning as the petrodollar system's enforcement mechanism.

projectRoles.role: The enforcement arm of petrodollar dominance, and simultaneously the mechanism accelerating its erosion. The sanctions stance is that dollar access is conditional on US-approved behavior. The mechanics: (1) because the global financial system runs on dollars, disconnection means economic strangulation — 'the financial equivalent of cutting off someone's oxygen supply,' (2) Iran's economy contracted 15% after 2012 sanctions, (3) Russia lost access to $300B in reserves in 2022. The paradox: sanctions work precisely because dollar dependency is so deep, but each use teaches the target and every observer to find alternatives. The 2022 Russia sanctions sent a message to every central bank: 'your dollar reserves are not yours — they can be confiscated.' This triggered record gold purchases and accelerated de-dollarization.

entities.name: De-Dollarization
entities.definition: Measurable global trend of reducing dollar dependency — dollar share of foreign exchange reserves dropping from 71% (2000) to 58% (2024), record central bank gold purchases (1,037 tonnes in 2023), China reducing Treasury holdings from $1.1T to under $800B, and construction of alternative payment infrastructure like CIPS and mBridge.

projectRoles.role: The macro-trend threatening the petrodollar system's future. De-dollarization's stance is gradual structural shift, not sudden rupture. The mechanics: (1) reserve share decline — 13 percentage points in 24 years, steady and unidirectional, (2) gold purchases at highest sustained levels since the 1960s (when France was demanding gold for dollars — a deliberate historical echo), (3) yuan's reserve share growing from 1% (2016) to 2.3% (2022) — small but with infrastructure being built, (4) BRICS coordination, bilateral currency swaps, local currency settlements all chip away at dollar centrality. The trend line is not ambiguous — the only question is speed. Three scenarios: slow erosion (most likely), strategic pivot (moderate probability), catastrophic break (low probability, maximum severity).

entities.name: Naval Mines
entities.definition: Iran's estimated arsenal of 2,000-5,000 naval mines — including Soviet-era contact mines, Chinese EM-52 rocket-propelled rising mines, and domestic variants — that represent the most cost-effective asymmetric weapon for chokepoint denial: a mine costs thousands of dollars, the supertanker it destroys costs $150 million, and clearing mines takes weeks while laying them takes hours.

projectRoles.project: The Strait of Hormuz: Military Chokepoint That Broke Global Energy
projectRoles.role: The ultimate asymmetric weapon whose economics define the Hormuz calculus. Mines' stance is strategic patience — they wait. The mechanics: (1) cost a few thousand dollars vs. $150M supertanker + $200M cargo, (2) can be laid from fishing boats and dhows indistinguishable from civilian traffic, (3) laying takes hours, clearing takes weeks with slow specialized minesweepers that are themselves vulnerable, (4) a carrier strike group cannot inspect every fishing boat in the Persian Gulf, (5) the Samuel B. Roberts (1988) and the 2026 mine-laying both prove the tactic remains viable across decades. Mine clearance is the most time-consuming operation in naval warfare — the math is entirely in Iran's favor.

entities.name: Operation Epic Fury
entities.definition: US and Israeli military operation beginning February 28, 2026 that struck Iranian targets including 130 IRGC naval vessels (100+ destroyed) and every Soleimani-class corvette — rendering the IRGCN 'combat ineffective' in conventional terms while simultaneously triggering Iran's asymmetric playbook of mines, coastal missiles, and insurance-market disruption that achieved the functional closure the conventional navy never could.

projectRoles.project: The Strait of Hormuz: Military Chokepoint That Broke Global Energy
projectRoles.role: The catalytic event that transformed a theoretical threat into an actual strait closure. Epic Fury's stance was conventional military dominance — destroy Iran's naval capability. The mechanics: (1) dozens of targets struck across Iran, (2) IRGC Navy a primary objective, (3) by Day 16 CENTCOM reported 130 vessels hit, 100+ destroyed, every Soleimani-class corvette sunk, (4) assessed as 'combat ineffective.' But the operation triggered what it intended to prevent: the IRGC activated the asymmetric playbook — mines, coastal missiles, and the phone call to Lloyd's — because retaliation was already underway, removing the restraint that had held for forty years. Epic Fury destroyed Iran's conventional capability while activating the unconventional doctrine that actually closed the strait.

entities.name: Operation Praying Mantis
entities.definition: Largest American naval engagement since World War II, launched April 18, 1988 in retaliation for the USS Samuel B. Roberts mine strike — US forces sank the Iranian frigate Sahand, disabled Sabalan, destroyed the Joshan, and demolished two IRGC oil platform staging bases, destroying half Iran's operational navy in eight hours and teaching Iran the lesson that reshaped its entire doctrine toward asymmetric warfare.

projectRoles.project: The Strait of Hormuz: Military Chokepoint That Broke Global Energy
projectRoles.role: The formative defeat that created Iran's asymmetric doctrine. Praying Mantis taught two different lessons to two different militaries: (1) Washington learned that overwhelming force works in the Gulf, (2) Tehran learned never to fight Americans on their terms — adapt, go asymmetric, make the strait itself the weapon. The mechanics of transformation: Iran conducted an extensive internal review and concluded the answer was not a bigger navy but a different kind of force — one that turned the strait's geography from vulnerability into weapon. Conventional naval warfare in a confined 21-mile waterway favors the defender. Every subsequent Iranian investment — swarm boats, mines, coastal missiles — traces directly to the Praying Mantis lesson.

entities.name: HMS Nemesis
entities.definition: Iron-hulled, steam-powered, flat-bottomed warship built in secret at Birkenhead, funded not by the Royal Navy but by the East India Company -- a private corporation's warship built with drug profits. Arrived in China in 1840 and systematically destroyed Chinese war junks, forts, and coastal defenses, navigating shallow rivers that Chinese forces assumed were natural barriers and firing Congreve rockets Chinese armies had never encountered.

projectRoles.role: The purest expression of the opium equation's closed loop: drug money funds military technology, military technology enforces market access, market access generates more drug money. HMS Nemesis demonstrates that a private drug-trading corporation could build and deploy a warship to destroy a sovereign nation's defenses in order to continue the drug trade. This was not state warfare in service of national interest but corporate warfare in service of revenue. The mechanics -- private funding, secret construction, technological superiority, deployed against a nation enforcing its own laws -- established the precedent that commercial interests can deploy military force to override sovereign drug policy.

entities.name: OPEC
entities.definition: Cartel of oil-producing nations that collectively controls a majority of global oil exports, whose adoption of dollar-only pricing — driven by Saudi Arabia's dominance as swing producer — transformed a bilateral US-Saudi deal into a global monetary system affecting every oil-importing nation on Earth.
aliases: Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries

projectRoles.role: The transmission mechanism that scaled the petrodollar from bilateral deal to global system. OPEC's stance follows Saudi Arabia's lead on pricing currency because Saudi Arabia controls swing production capacity. The mechanics: when Saudi Arabia priced in dollars, Kuwait, UAE, Iraq, Iran, Venezuela, Nigeria, and Libya followed within two years — making virtually all 40 million barrels/day of global oil dollar-denominated. This wasn't a democratic choice but a structural inevitability: the swing producer's decision became every member's constraint. OPEC's collective dollar pricing forces every oil-importing nation on Earth to maintain dollar reserves, creating the permanent artificial demand that underpins the entire system.

entities.name: ICSID
entities.definition: International arbitration body housed inside the World Bank that adjudicates investment disputes between corporations and sovereign nations — including Bechtel's twenty-five million dollar lawsuit against Bolivia after being expelled from Cochabamba — creating a closed loop where the institution that required privatization also judges disputes arising from privatization.
aliases: International Centre for Settlement of Investment Disputes

projectRoles.role: The judicial mechanism that completes the institutional closed loop. ICSID's stance is investor protection through international arbitration. The mechanics: (1) housed inside the World Bank — the same institution that required privatization, (2) corporations can sue nations for changing water policy, (3) nations cannot sue corporations for failing to deliver water, (4) Bechtel used ICSID to sue Bolivia for lost future profits. The chain: World Bank required privatization, Bechtel got the contract, Bolivia cancelled it, Bechtel sued at the World Bank's own court. 'The institution that created the problem is adjudicating the complaint about the solution.'

entities.name: Fiscal Multiplier Error
entities.definition: The 2013 discovery by IMF Chief Economist Olivier Blanchard that the fiscal multiplier used in Greek crisis calculations was between 0.9-1.7, not the assumed 0.5 — meaning austerity was nearly twice as destructive as the IMF's own models predicted, prescribed doses based on calculations the institution later admitted were wrong.

projectRoles.project: The IMF: Lender of Last Resort
projectRoles.role: The mathematical proof that the institution's own models were miscalibrated with devastating consequences. The error's stance is that incorrect assumptions hardcoded into lending models produce real-world suffering. The mechanics: (1) the IMF assumed cutting one euro of government spending reduces GDP by 50 cents (multiplier 0.5), (2) the Blanchard paper found actual multiplier was 0.9-1.7, (3) this means every euro of cuts produced 80 cents to $1.70 of GDP loss — not 50 cents, (4) Greece's 25% GDP contraction, 27.5% unemployment, 60% youth unemployment, and 35% increase in suicide rates were the human cost of wrong math. The paper changed the academic debate. It did not undo the damage.

entities.name: US Veto Power
entities.definition: The structural guarantee arising from the intersection of the 85% supermajority requirement for fundamental IMF decisions and the US holding 16.5% of votes — meaning one country can block any reform, a power no other nation possesses, preserved through every quota review for eighty-two years.

projectRoles.project: The IMF: Lender of Last Resort
projectRoles.role: The single most important architectural feature preventing IMF reform. The veto's stance is permanent minority control through threshold design. The mechanics: (1) the threshold was set at Bretton Woods when the US had overwhelming leverage, (2) any quota reallocation pushing the US below 15% eliminates its blocking power — no administration has agreed to this, (3) the veto means developing countries can push for rebalancing indefinitely without effect, (4) the structure ensures the institution cannot evolve beyond its 1944 design without US consent. The veto is not a bug — it is the foundational feature that makes all other structural asymmetries permanent.

entities.name: Abqaiq-Khurais Attack
entities.definition: September 14, 2019 drone and cruise missile attack on Saudi Aramco's Abqaiq and Khurais oil processing facilities — the world's largest oil processing complex — using 18 drones and 7 cruise missiles to knock 5.7 million barrels/day offline in a single strike (half of Saudi output, 5% of global supply), spiking oil 15% in one trading session.

projectRoles.project: The Strait of Hormuz: Military Chokepoint That Broke Global Energy
projectRoles.role: The reconnaissance strike that mapped the system's pressure points before the main assault. The Abqaiq attack's stance was proof of concept. The mechanics: (1) 18 drones + 7 cruise missiles = $50M+ damage to the world's largest oil processing complex, (2) 5.7M barrels/day knocked offline — half of Saudi output, 5% of global supply, (3) oil spiked 15% in a single trading session, (4) Houthis claimed it, US/UK/France/Germany attributed it to Iran, (5) the attack was not meant to start a war — it was reconnaissance: mapping pressure points, testing insurance market response, measuring price movements, observing US military reaction. The IRGC was studying the machine before deciding to break it.

entities.name: Harry Dexter White
entities.definition: Assistant Secretary of the US Treasury who designed the dollar-centered international monetary architecture at Bretton Woods in 1944 — defeating Keynes's bancor proposal by leveraging America's postwar economic dominance — later accused of passing information to Soviet intelligence and died of a heart attack in 1948, three days after testifying before the House Un-American Activities Committee.

projectRoles.project: The IMF: Lender of Last Resort
projectRoles.role: The ghost architect whose design outlived his loyalties. White's stance was American financial dominance embedded in institutional architecture. The mechanics: (1) proposed the US dollar as anchor with all currencies pegged to the dollar pegged to gold, (2) designed the quota-weighted voting system that gave the US permanent structural advantage, (3) won not because his plan was better but because the US had the leverage, (4) the Venona project declassified Soviet cables corroborating at least some contacts with Soviet intelligence. The architect of American financial hegemony may have been a Soviet agent — but the machine outlived its maker's loyalties. The system he built entrenched dollar dominance regardless of who he reported to.

entities.name: Greek Debt Crisis
entities.definition: Crisis triggered by Greece's 2010 revelation that its deficit was 15.4% of GDP (not the reported 3.7%) — resulting in three troika bailout packages totaling EUR 289 billion with severe austerity that contracted GDP by 25%, pushed unemployment to 27.5% and youth unemployment past 60%, while the IMF's own models later proved the fiscal multiplier was nearly twice as destructive as assumed.

projectRoles.project: The IMF: Lender of Last Resort
projectRoles.role: The wrong-math case study — proof that the institution's own models were miscalibrated. The crisis's stance is that austerity prescribed on incorrect calculations produces Great Depression-level damage. The mechanics: (1) the troika (IMF + ECB + European Commission) prescribed 30% public sector wage cuts, pension cuts, VAT increases, mass layoffs, privatization of ports and airports, (2) the IMF's models assumed cutting one euro of spending reduces GDP by 50 cents (multiplier 0.5), (3) the 2013 Blanchard paper found the actual multiplier was 0.9-1.7 — austerity was nearly twice as destructive as the IMF predicted, (4) suicide rates increased 35%, the contraction was comparable to the American Great Depression. The institution prescribed a dose based on calculations it later admitted were wrong.

entities.name: Asian Financial Crisis
entities.definition: Financial crisis beginning with Thailand's baht collapse in July 1997 that spread to Indonesia, South Korea, Malaysia, and the Philippines — prompting IMF interventions totaling $116+ billion with standard austerity conditions that deepened the crisis, most devastatingly in Indonesia where GDP contracted 13.1% and poverty doubled after IMF-mandated bank closures triggered depositor panic.

projectRoles.project: The IMF: Lender of Last Resort
projectRoles.role: The wrong-medicine case study that produced the most enduring critique of IMF prescriptions. The crisis's stance is that standard conditionality applied to a liquidity crisis is like 'administering aspirin to a patient with internal bleeding' (Stiglitz). The mechanics: (1) IMF prescribed fiscal austerity, high interest rates, and immediate bank closures during a capital flight crisis, (2) in Indonesia, closing 16 banks triggered depositor panic across all remaining banks — the cure caused the disease, (3) raising interest rates during a liquidity crisis choked economies that needed oxygen, (4) Malaysia refused the IMF program, imposed capital controls (the exact opposite prescription), and recovered faster. The Camdessus-Suharto photograph — the IMF director arms-crossed while Suharto signs — became the portrait of institutional humiliation across Asia.

entities.name: Greece
entities.definition: Nation that revealed a government deficit of 15.4% of GDP in 2010 (previously reported as 3.7%), triggering three troika bailout packages totaling EUR 289 billion with severe austerity conditions that contracted GDP by 25%, pushed unemployment to 27.5% and youth unemployment past 60%, increased suicide rates 35% — damage comparable to the American Great Depression.

projectRoles.project: The IMF: Lender of Last Resort
projectRoles.role: The wrong-math case study — where the institution's miscalibrated models produced Great Depression-level damage in a European democracy. Greece's stance was forced compliance with devastating conditions. The mechanics: (1) the troika prescribed 30% wage cuts, pension cuts, mass layoffs, privatization, (2) the fiscal multiplier assumption was wrong by a factor of 2x — austerity was nearly twice as destructive as modeled, (3) 25% GDP contraction, 27.5% unemployment, 35% suicide increase, (4) the IMF acknowledged the error only after the damage was done. Greece demonstrates that the conditionality system's harm is not limited to developing nations — given sufficient miscalculation, it can produce Great Depression outcomes in advanced economies.

entities.name: US Treasury
entities.definition: The IMF's largest shareholder and most powerful external influence — providing the institutional and ideological framework for conditionality policy, holding 16.5% of IMF votes, and forming one vertex of the Washington Consensus triangle alongside the IMF and World Bank.

projectRoles.project: The IMF: Lender of Last Resort
projectRoles.role: The power behind the institution. The US Treasury's stance is creditor-first financial orthodoxy. The mechanics: (1) Harry Dexter White was Assistant Secretary of the Treasury — the IMF was literally designed by Treasury staff, (2) forms the third vertex of the Washington Consensus alongside IMF and World Bank, (3) holds the largest quota and therefore largest voting share, (4) every major IMF decision requires US Treasury acquiescence because of the veto power. The Treasury-IMF-World Bank triangle is the institutional expression of American financial dominance — designed by the Treasury, governed through the Treasury's voting power.

The government's financial arm, distinct from but intertwined with the central bank. The Treasury's presence at Jekyll Island through Andrew shows that even the Fed's secret design included government participation — the boundary between fiscal and monetary policy has always been porous.

entities.name: Washington Consensus
entities.definition: Term coined by economist John Williamson in 1989 for the ten policy prescriptions that Washington institutions (IMF, World Bank, US Treasury) agreed on for developing countries — fiscal discipline, privatization, deregulation, trade liberalization, and six others — that became the rigid default template applied to every country in crisis regardless of circumstance.

projectRoles.project: The IMF: Lender of Last Resort
projectRoles.role: The ideological framework that turned institutional preference into universal prescription. The Washington Consensus's stance is one-size-fits-all market orthodoxy. The mechanics: (1) ten prescriptions covering fiscal, monetary, trade, and structural policy, (2) Williamson protested his term was hijacked to describe rigid free-market ideology he never endorsed, (3) between 1980-2000 the template was applied to 100+ countries through structural adjustment programs, (4) Sub-Saharan Africa's GDP per capita was lower in 2000 than in 1980 — two decades of adjustment, negative results, (5) the IMF's own Independent Evaluation Office admitted in 2011 that conditionality was 'too intrusive' and 'insufficiently sensitive to country circumstances.' The template was the problem — treating different diseases with the same medicine.

entities.name: US Treasury Bonds
entities.definition: US government debt instruments that serve as the primary recycling destination for petrodollars — Saudi and Gulf sovereign wealth funds invest hundreds of billions in Treasuries, providing the US government with structurally guaranteed low-interest loans funded by the very money America spent on oil imports.

projectRoles.role: The capital recycling endpoint of the petrodollar system. Treasuries' stance is as the 'safest' dollar-denominated asset — but this safety is architecturally created, not earned. The mechanics: (1) oil-exporting nations accumulate massive dollar surpluses, (2) the safest and most liquid place to park dollars is US Treasuries, (3) this creates structurally guaranteed demand for US government debt regardless of fiscal discipline, (4) the result: America borrows at rates no other debtor could command because the demand is not voluntary but architectural. The threat: as central banks diversify reserves (gold purchases at record levels 2022-2024, China reducing Treasury holdings), this structural demand is eroding — threatening the cheap borrowing that funds everything from the military to social programs.

entities.name: US Defense Industry
entities.definition: American weapons manufacturers — Lockheed Martin, Boeing, Raytheon, General Dynamics — that function as monetary recycling endpoints, channeling petrodollars back to the US through over $100 billion in Saudi arms purchases since 2010 alone, with tens of billions more from UAE, Kuwait, and Qatar.

projectRoles.role: The weapons channel of petrodollar recycling. The defense industry's stance is commercial — sell advanced weapons systems — but its systemic function is monetary return. The mechanics: (1) F-15 Eagles, Patriot missiles, AWACS, M1 Abrams tanks, guided munitions, training programs, maintenance contracts, (2) over $100 billion from Saudi Arabia since 2010 alone, plus tens of billions from UAE, Kuwait, Qatar, (3) every arms purchase is petrodollar recycling — dollars that left America to buy oil return through defense contractors, (4) the guns protect the oil states, the oil states fund the guns — the loop is seamless. The defense industry isn't just building weapons; it's operating as a monetary recycling endpoint.

entities.name: Dow
entities.definition: American chemical corporation that, along with DuPont, had enormous production capacity after World War II and needed new markets — since ammonium nitrate makes both explosives and fertilizer, the developing world's agricultural modernization was 'not just an opportunity but a survival strategy for an industry built for conflict.'

projectRoles.role: One of the chemical industry actors whose postwar surplus capacity drove the fertilizer and pesticide markets that the Green Revolution depended on. Dow and DuPont demonstrate the military-industrial-agricultural nexus: wartime chemistry became peacetime agriculture, not through humanitarian intent but through market necessity.

entities.name: DuPont
entities.definition: American chemical corporation that alongside Dow had massive wartime production capacity repurposed for agricultural chemicals — part of the military-to-agriculture pipeline where wartime munitions manufacturing became peacetime fertilizer and pesticide production.

projectRoles.role: The other half of the chemical industry pivot from war to agriculture. DuPont's postwar conversion from munitions to fertilizer demonstrates that the Green Revolution's chemical input system was not designed for agriculture — it was adapted from military production. The molecular structure of ammonium nitrate doesn't care about intentions.

entities.name: Jimmy Carter
entities.definition: President who appointed Paul Volcker as Federal Reserve chairman in August 1979 to fight 14.8% inflation — a decision that would prove politically costly as Volcker's 20% interest rates caused severe recession, demonstrating the tension between presidential appointment power and central bank independence.

projectRoles.role: The president whose appointment enabled the most aggressive independent central bank action in American history. Carter appointed Volcker knowing tough measures were needed, but the resulting economic pain contributed to his political difficulties — illustrating that presidents who empower independent central bankers may not survive the political consequences.

entities.name: Sanae Takaichi
entities.definition: Japanese Prime Minister who won a supermajority of 316 seats in the February 2026 snap election, campaigning on loose monetary policy — creating direct political pressure on Bank of Japan Governor Ueda who is trying to normalize rates at 0.75%, the highest since 1995.

projectRoles.role: The Japanese vector of the global independence challenge. Takaichi's supermajority gives her enormous political leverage over the BOJ — illustrating that the independence question is not just an American problem but a global pattern where political leaders want control of rates because loose money wins elections.

entities.name: Kazuo Ueda
entities.definition: Bank of Japan Governor trying to normalize interest rates at 0.75% — the highest since 1995 — after forty-five months above the inflation target, while facing political pressure from Prime Minister Takaichi who campaigned on loose monetary policy.

projectRoles.role: The technocrat versus the politician. Ueda represents the central banker trying to do what the data says (normalize rates after decades of zero) while elected officials want the opposite (keep rates low). His position is the investigation's independence doctrine under real-time stress test.

entities.name: Great Depression
entities.definition: Economic catastrophe of the 1930s that Ben Bernanke studied extensively before becoming Fed Chair — understanding what happens when central banks fail to act — and the standard against which every subsequent crisis is measured to justify central bank intervention.

projectRoles.role: The historical benchmark for central bank failure. The Great Depression's lesson — that central bank inaction can turn recession into catastrophe — justifies every subsequent expansion of central bank power. Bernanke became Fed Chair specifically because he understood this lesson, and his 2008 interventions were explicitly informed by what went wrong in the 1930s.

entities.name: Revolving Door Problem
entities.definition: The pattern where the same countries return to the IMF repeatedly — Sri Lanka 17 times since 1965, Pakistan 23 times since 1958, Argentina across four decades — raising the structural question of whether conditional lending that treats symptoms without resolving causes guarantees the borrower will return, producing the system the IMF itself calls a 'revolving door problem.'

projectRoles.project: The IMF: Lender of Last Resort
projectRoles.role: The investigation's central insight — the shift from 'what is wrong with these countries' to 'what kind of machine produces repeat customers.' The revolving door's stance is structural inevitability. The mechanics form a self-reinforcing loop: (1) cut spending to close the deficit during crisis, (2) the cut reduces economic activity, (3) reduced activity reduces revenue, (4) the deficit returns, (5) the country borrows again, (6) conditions are reimposed, (7) the cycle continues. The IMF acknowledges this pattern. Critics call it a debt trap — not conspiratorial but structural. The machine produces the outcome it was designed to produce: countries that keep borrowing from an institution governed by countries that never borrow.

entities.name: Concession Agreement System
entities.definition: The contractual architecture through which water privatization operates — typically featuring 30-40 year exclusive operation rights, guaranteed minimum revenue (government pays if customers can't), currency fluctuation protection (government absorbs exchange rate risk), and the right to international arbitration under bilateral investment treaties — creating asymmetric contracts where corporations can sue nations but nations cannot sue corporations.

projectRoles.role: The legal mechanism that makes water privatization structurally asymmetric. The concession system's mechanics: (1) exclusive operation rights for 30-40 years, (2) guaranteed minimum revenue — meaning the government pays the corporation if customers can't afford the prices, (3) currency fluctuation protection shifts exchange rate risk to the government, (4) international arbitration rights allow corporations to sue sovereign nations for changing water policy. A corporation can sue a nation for changing water policy. The nation cannot sue the corporation for failing to deliver water. The investigation's instruction: 'Read that again.'

entities.name: United Nations General Assembly
entities.definition: UN body that passed Resolution 64/292 on July 28, 2010 recognizing water as a human right — with 122 votes in favor, none against, 41 abstentions — producing a non-binding resolution that created symbolic recognition without enforcement mechanism.

projectRoles.role: The institutional body that produced the symbolic recognition of water as a human right. The UNGA's vote demonstrates near-universal acknowledgment (122 yes, 0 no) but the 41 abstentions and non-binding nature reveal the gap between acknowledgment and enforcement. The investigation notes: 'There is applause. There are photographs. There is a press release. There is no enforcement mechanism.'

entities.name: Alan Greenspan
entities.definition: Fed Chair for nineteen years (1987-2006) — the longest tenure since the Fed's founding — who kept rates low after every crisis (1987 crash, 1997 Asian crisis, 2001 dot-com bust), training markets to believe the Fed would always rescue them and creating moral hazard at systemic scale that inflated the housing bubble he left for his successor.

projectRoles.role: The cautionary tale of too much market confidence in central bank rescue. Greenspan's tenure created the 'Greenspan Put' — the belief that the Fed would bail out any downturn — which produced moral hazard: banks took bigger risks because they believed the central bank would catch them. The housing bubble inflated between 2003 and 2006, and when Greenspan retired, 'the bomb is already built. His successor will inherit the detonation.'

entities.name: Lehman Brothers
entities.definition: Investment bank whose September 2008 collapse froze the global financial system — banks stopped lending, credit markets seized — triggering the chain of Federal Reserve interventions that expanded the central bank's role from lender of last resort to buyer of last resort and launched the era of quantitative easing.

projectRoles.role: The trigger event for the central bank's permanent expansion. Lehman Brothers' collapse is the investigation's inflection point: before Lehman, the Fed was a backstop; after Lehman, the Fed became a market maker willing to create trillions from nothing. Everything that followed — QE, $8 trillion in asset purchases, the COVID response — traces back to the precedent set after Lehman fell.

entities.name: Ben Bernanke
entities.definition: Scholar of the Great Depression who became Fed Chair specifically because he understood what happens when central banks fail to act — and who 'crossed the Rubicon' in 2008 by expanding the Fed from lender of last resort to buyer of last resort, launching quantitative easing that grew the balance sheet from $891 billion to $4.5 trillion.

projectRoles.role: The central banker who permanently expanded the role of the institution. Bernanke's 2008 decisions set the precedent that when the crisis is severe enough, the central bank will create trillions from nothing: (1) cut rates to zero, (2) launched QE when that wasn't enough, (3) expanded the Fed's role from lender to buyer to market maker of last resort. The financial system survived but the question of who absorbs the consequences was 'left for later.'

entities.name: Main Street
entities.definition: Conceptual shorthand for the ordinary economy — mortgages, hiring, small businesses, consumer spending — that receives central bank policy benefits last because the transmission mechanism flows through financial markets first, reaching asset owners immediately and everyone else eventually.

projectRoles.role: The investigation's measure of who benefits last from central bank action. Main Street versus Wall Street is the plumbing problem: (1) Fed cuts rates or launches QE, (2) bond and stock prices rise immediately, (3) by the time cheaper borrowing reaches Main Street, months or years have passed. The people who benefit first own financial assets. This is not conspiracy — it is plumbing.

entities.name: Wealth Inequality Mechanism
entities.definition: The structural transmission problem of central bank policy: when the Fed cuts rates or launches QE, money flows through financial markets first — bond prices, stock prices, real estate rise immediately — while cheaper borrowing reaches ordinary people months or years later. The top 10% own 89% of stock market wealth; between 2020 and 2022, billionaire wealth increased by $1.7 trillion while bottom 50% wages barely kept pace with inflation.

projectRoles.role: The investigation's core critique of central banking mechanics. This is not conspiracy but plumbing: (1) policy transmits through asset markets, (2) those closest to the pipes get the water first, (3) QE was the largest upward wealth transfer in modern history — not by design, but by mechanism. The tool works. The plumbing is the issue. The question is whether an institution that systematically benefits asset owners first can claim to serve the entire economy.

entities.name: Six-Stage Extraction Cycle
